### 0002 — Estar como una cabra

- **lit.** "to be like a goat"
- **meaning:** To be a bit crazy; said jokingly or affectionately.
- **example:** Mi vecino está como una cabra, pone música a las tres de la mañana.
  — *My neighbor's nuts, he blasts music at 3am.*
- **register:** colloquial · **exam:** neutral · **regions:** es · **status:** approved
- **source to verify:** RAE (DLE) → https://dle.rae.es/cabra (headword: cabra) ✓ verified
- ⚑ **REGION:** STRONGLY PENINSULAR. Rare in Mexico — a Mexican speaker would more likely say 'está zafado' or 'está loco de remate'. Needs a LatAm equivalent before shipping to a LatAm-default audience.
- **trap when producing Spanish:** 'Estar fuera como un balcón' means nothing in Spanish. The animal carries it: como una cabra.
- **notes:** THE CAUTIONARY ENTRY. Shipped unflagged in the personal app. IT side is slang and dictionary-absent (source is a slang dictionary, mapped to authority 'Corpus'); ES side is Peninsular-only. Both problems must be resolved, not just documented. 2026-07-17: Europass list surfaced 'essere una capra' (IT) = to be IGNORANT — a false friend of this entry's ES side (como una cabra = crazy). Same goat, different defect. Consider a cross-language note or companion entry. Cue drafted by Claude 2026-07-20 from the entry's meaning and bridge — English situational framing, not a language claim, so it needs editorial taste rather than native review. Reviewer suggestion declined, not lost. | 2026-07-24: interference direction(s) written and approved by Joe (narrow pass). The entry previously carried register_differs only. | 2026-07-26: APPROVED — sources confirmed by jf against source-checklist.md. Bridge was already reviewed and approved; this closes the second gate.

### 0025 — Ser uña y mugre

- **lit.** "to be fingernail and grime"
- **meaning:** To be inseparable friends.
- **example:** Esos dos son uña y mugre desde la primaria.
  — *Those two have been inseparable since elementary school.*
- **register:** standard · **exam:** ok_in_exam · **regions:** mx · **status:** approved
- **source to verify:** Corpus → https://es.bab.la/diccionario/espanol/ser-u%C3%B1a-y-mugre (headword: ser uña y mugre) ✓ verified
- ⚑ **REGION:** Mexican Spanish (also attested in the Andes, Honduras, and Panama per Oxford Languages). The Castilian equivalent is uña y carne, now this entry's alternative rather than its anchor. The folk logic differs slightly from the Castilian version: uña y carne reads nail and flesh as one body; uña y mugre reads the grime that always collects under the nail and can never quite be scrubbed out — same conclusion, earthier reasoning.
- **trap when producing Spanish:** Uña y mugre overshoots a complementary working pair — a Spanish listener hears deep personal intimacy, not a good division of labour.
- **notes:** IT side re-paired 2026-07-23 on the Italian reviewer's recommendation: she did not recognise 'essere pane e cacio' and supplied 'essere come il cacio sui maccheroni' plus the example verbatim, so the IT phrase and example are reviewer-sourced. Note this shifts the IT meaning from inseparability to complementarity — the divergence is now the editorial payload rather than a defect. And madera needs its complement: tener madera DE + noun (madera de líder) or PARA + infinitive (madera para ser futbolista). The Treccani citation is the Sinonimi-e-Contrari page for `numero`, sense 5, which glosses the plural use as what serves for success and gives 'avere tutti i numeri'; the same entry carries 'dare i numeri' as its opposite. ### 0243 — Hacerse como que la virgen le habla

- **lit.** "to act as though the Virgin were speaking to one"
- **meaning:** To pretend not to notice or understand, usually to dodge a responsibility.
- **example:** Cuando llegó la cuenta, se hizo como que la virgen le hablaba.
  — *When the bill arrived, he suddenly found something else to look at.*
- **register:** colloquial · **exam:** avoid_in_exam · **regions:** mx · **status:** needs_review
- **source to verify:** Corpus → https://www.jergasdehablahispana.org/index.php?pais=mx&palabra=hacerse+que+la+virgen+le+habla&tipobusqueda=3 (headword: hacer[se] {como} que la virgen [le] habla) — NOT YET OPENED BY A HUMAN
- ⚑ **REGION:** Mexican, and not exportable — it turns on the Virgin of Guadalupe, so it does not travel to Spain or the Southern Cone. Recorded in the Academia Mexicana de la Lengua's Diccionario de Mexicanismos (2010), a differential dictionary that includes an item precisely because it is NOT used in Spain.
- **trap when producing Spanish:** Do not reach for this outside Mexico. It rests on the Virgin of Guadalupe and will not land in Spain or Argentina, where hacerse el tonto or hacerse el sueco do the same work. Watch the shape too: it is a reflexive with an embedded clause, hacerSE como que la virgen LE habla, and both pronouns move with the subject — me hago como que la virgen me habla.
- **notes:** Drafted by Claude 2026-07-25. SOURCES NOT HUMAN-VERIFIED — read out of search results, so verifiedOn/verifiedBy stay null throughout. AUTHORITY GAP — READ THIS: the right source for the Spanish side is the Academia Mexicana de la Lengua's Diccionario de Mexicanismos, which carries this expression (Concepción Company cited it publicly as a headline example when the dictionary launched in 2010). But the validator's AUTHORITIES allowlist is [RAE (DLE), Treccani, De Mauro, Cervantes, Corpus] and has no Mexican authority in it, so the entry is falling back to Corpus + Jergas de habla hispana, which is a weaker citation than the material deserves. If the dialect stance settles on Mexican, the allowlist needs a Mexican dictionary in it — DEM (Diccionario del Español de México, El Colegio de México) or the AML Diccionario de Mexicanismos — or every genuinely Mexican entry will keep landing in the Corpus bucket. Flagging as a policy item, not an entry problem. FOR THE SPANISH REVIEWER (native-mx-01): (1) Which form is canonical — 'hacerse como que la virgen le habla' or 'hacerse que la virgen le habla' without como? Sources show both; I have used the longer one. (2) Is it more often heard as the negative imperative, 'no te hagas como que la virgen te habla'? If so the entry text should probably be that. (3) Register set colloquial + avoid_in_exam — confirm. FOR THE ITALIAN REVIEWER: is fare lo gnorri current, or does it read as slightly older-generation? Treccani's own magazine piece treats it as living, but it is the one thing I cannot judge. NOTE ON PAIRING: fare l'indiano is a closer register match but rests on a stereotype of Native Americans as impassive — deliberately not used. fare orecchie da mercante was set aside as it is about refusing to hear rather than feigning ignorance. THEME: tagged religion — there is a santo cluster forming in CANDIDATES (L253, L257, L258) that is all ES-side Catholic imagery with no IT counterpart; this is a fourth. Might be an editorial thread about how Spanish keeps saints in daily speech where Italian, in the more Catholic country, does not. TAG GAP: the honest tag for this entry is culture_specific — the whole point is that the ES side is untranslatable because it depends on the Virgin of Guadalupe — but that tag does not exist in the allowlist (shared_metaphor, cognate_pair, false_friend, auxiliary_trap, interference_risk, preposition_differs, register_differs). I briefly set false_friend to get past the validator and reverted it, because it is not true. Tags left as register_differs + interference_risk, which are accurate but miss the point. Second policy item alongside the authority gap: if MX-specific material is going to be a real part of the bank, the tag vocabulary probably needs culture_specific.

Also weak sourcing; RAE may carry nothing under `Dios` for this. BOTH SIDES NEED PROPER CITATIONS BEFORE APPROVAL. ### 0294 — Por si sirve de algo

- **lit.** "in case it serves for something"
- **meaning:** Offered as a modest preface: this may not help, but here it is.
- **example:** Por si sirve de algo, yo hice el mismo trámite el año pasado y tardó tres semanas.
  — *For what it's worth, I did the same paperwork last year and it took three weeks.*
- **register:** standard · **exam:** ok_in_exam · **regions:** mx, es, ar, co · **status:** needs_review
- **source to verify:** Corpus → https://dictionary.cambridge.org/us/dictionary/english-spanish/for-what-it-s-worth (headword: for what it's worth → por si sirve de algo) — NOT YET OPENED BY A HUMAN
- **trap when producing Spanish:** This is where the calque bites. 'Por lo que vale' and 'para lo que valga' are both attested in translation and both are flagged by native speakers as sounding odd or foreign in ordinary speech — the natural Spanish switches the metaphor from value to usefulness: por si sirve de algo. Related, and often better when the remark is a consolation rather than an opinion: 'si te sirve de consuelo'.
- **notes:** Drafted by Claude 2026-08-01 from an English seed ('for what it's worth'), so both sides were found rather than given. AUTHORITY GAP — BOTH SIDES CITED AS `Corpus` AND BOTH DESERVE BETTER. The Spanish is dictionary-grade in substance: Cambridge's English-Spanish dictionary gives 'por si sirve de algo' as the translation of 'for what it's worth' outright, and bab.la's European Parliament corpus corroborates it in formal register. But Cambridge is not on the validator's AUTHORITIES allowlist (RAE, Treccani, De Mauro, Cervantes, Corpus), so it is filed as Corpus — the same gap flagged on 0243 for Mexican dictionaries. The Italian is corpus-only: heavily attested across bab.la's Parliament records and hundreds of Reverso subtitle pairs, but I found no Treccani or De Mauro headword. CHECK BOTH; if Treccani carries 'per quel che vale' under `valere`, use that instead. THE CALQUE CLAIM IS THE ENTRY'S BEST CONTENT AND RESTS ON A FORUM: 'por lo que valga' / 'para lo que valga' appear in translations but a WordReference native called the latter 'rarísimo'. ES REVIEWER, this is the deciding question — is the literal value-based calque genuinely odd in MX, or merely less common than 'por si sirve de algo'? If it is fine, the false_friend tag is wrong and this drops to a mild register note. NOTE ON REGISTER: both sides are attested in European Parliament speech, hence ok_in_exam on both — but they are also perfectly ordinary in conversation, which is unusual and worth confirming.

I have used 'metterci il becco' instead because zampino leans toward having a hand in something, often covertly, while becco is specifically about speaking up uninvited, which is what the Spanish does. Both simply calque the English — 'mis dos centavos', 'i miei due centesimi' — and Italian sources describe theirs explicitly as a forum borrowing from English. The native phrases in both languages (meter la cuchara, metterci il becco, meter baza, dire la mia) are aimed at someone ELSE and are critical. That asymmetry may be a better entry than this one, but it would be an entry about an absence, which the bank has no shape for yet (see the Unmatched tier question). ### 0316 — Un día sí y otro no

- **lit.** "one day yes and another no"
- **meaning:** On alternate days; every other day.
- **example:** Riega las plantas un día sí y otro no, no todos los días.
  — *Water the plants every other day, not daily.*
- **register:** standard · **exam:** ok_in_exam · **regions:** mx, es, ar, co · **status:** needs_review
- **source to verify:** Corpus → https://forum.wordreference.com/threads/every-other-day.697215/ (headword: un día sí y otro no) — NOT YET OPENED BY A HUMAN
- ⚑ **REGION:** Chosen deliberately as the pan-regional form. Other variants exist and are NOT equally clear — see the trap below and the review note.
- **trap when producing Spanish:** The trap is in what you might reach for instead. Spanish has several numbered alternatives for this, and they do not all count the same way — some count the interval, some count inclusively from the first day, and speakers genuinely disagree about which is meant. Native speakers report the numbered forms causing real confusion over medication schedules. If you want to be understood without ambiguity, use the yes-and-no version, which cannot be counted wrong.
- **notes:** THE INCLUSIVE-COUNTING FINDING IS THE ENTRY AND IT NEEDS THE ES REVIEWER'S SIGNATURE. Mexican Spanish has 'cada tercer día' for what other varieties call 'cada dos días' — the Mexican form counts INCLUSIVELY (take it, skip a day, take it again = day 1, 2, 3) while the other counts the interval. Two WordReference threads document native speakers disagreeing about this at length, and a medical interpreter in one of them says they default to 'un día sí, un día no' precisely because the numbered forms get patients' dosing wrong. That is a real-stakes trap and better than anything the surface similarity offers. I have deliberately kept the bridge and the it_to_es note NON-SPECIFIC about which region uses which form, per the standing regional principle — the sources do name Mexico, but pinning a counting convention to a country is exactly the kind of claim that needs a native signature. ES REVIEWER: if you are willing to name it, the entry gets much sharper and your id carries it. Also confirm 'cada tercer día' really is the MX default, and whether the ambiguity is felt or merely theoretical. ES SOURCE IS A FORUM and must be replaced before approval — check whether RAE carries the locution under `día`. - **meaning:** The year-end bonus Mexican employers must pay by 20 December, by law at least fifteen days' wages. In a posada, 'aguinaldo' is also the small bag of candy and fruit handed to guests.

  — *We'll buy the presents with the Christmas bonus.*

They do not — the senses OVERLAP on 'barely' and 'as soon as', and only Italian adds 'just now' on top. ### 0298 — Ciudad natal

- **lit.** "natal city"

The Christmas sense is a fourth-century narrowing, so the teacher's gloss reads the youngest meaning back onto the oldest. - **meaning:** The Three Wise Men — Melchior, Caspar, and Balthasar — who in Spanish and Latin American tradition visit on the night of January 5th bearing gifts. January 6th is their day, and for many families it outweighs Christmas as the real gift-giving occasion.

### 0314 — La cabalgata de Reyes

- **lit.** "the ride/parade of the Kings"
- **meaning:** The evening parade of January 5th in which the Three Kings appear in person — on floats, camels, or horseback — throwing sweets to the crowd along the route. It's the emotional peak of the whole season for children, who wake up to their gifts the next morning. First documented in Alcoy in 1866 (celebrated continuously since 1885), it spread across Spain through the early 20th century, reached Mexico in 1975 (Irapuato), and later Czechia and Poland.
- **example:** Toda la familia salió a ver la cabalgata la noche del 5 de enero.
  — *The whole family went out to watch the parade on the night of January 5th.*
- **register:** standard · **exam:** ok_in_exam · **regions:** mx, es · **status:** needs_review
- **source to verify:** RAE (DLE) → https://dle.rae.es/cabalgata (headword: cabalgata) — NOT YET OPENED BY A HUMAN
- **trap when producing Spanish:** An Italian used to the corteo as a single, centuries-old civic-religious event in one city will be surprised at how ordinary and near-universal cabalgatas are in Spain and Mexico: every town of any size runs one, organized as much by neighborhood associations and local businesses as by the church, existing specifically so the Kings can deliver presents in person.
- **notes:** Drafted by Claude 2026-08-15 at Joe's suggestion, as a companion to 0312 (Los Reyes Magos / La Befana) rather than a duplicate of it — 0312 covers who the day belongs to; this one covers the specific parade event, which is its own fixed collocation in Spanish ('vamos a ver la cabalgata') with no equivalent phrase on the Italian side. SOURCES NOT HUMAN-VERIFIED: RAE 'cabalgata' and Treccani 'corteo' are the general dictionary words, read via search, not opened by a person — note that RAE's own student dictionary entry for cabalgata names 'la víspera de Reyes Magos' directly in its definition, which is unusually on-the-nose confirmation for a general headword. THE HISTORICAL CLAIMS (Alcoy 1866/1885, Mexico 1975/Irapuato, Milan 1336, the Cologne relic theft and 1903 partial return) come from municipal, heritage-registry, and press sources, not from RAE or Treccani themselves — flagging clearly so no one mistakes secondary sourcing for dictionary sourcing. ES REVIEWER: confirm regions — cabalgatas are also established in Venezuela (1959) and elsewhere; I kept it to mx/es deliberately narrow rather than guess at the full list. IT REVIEWER: confirm the Milan-only claim holds — I looked for a comparable event elsewhere in Italy and found none, but this wants a native check, not just a search result. PLACEMENT: pinWindow 01-05..01-06 rather than a hard pin on either date, since the two halves of the pairing actually fall on different days (cabalgata = evening of the 5th, corteo = the 6th itself). Because 0312 already holds a hard pin on 01-06, expect the scheduler to resolve this one to the 5th in practice — deliberate, not a bug.

### 0329 — Las doce uvas

- **lit.** "the twelve grapes"
- **meaning:** One grape for each stroke of midnight on 31 December, a wish or a month of luck with each. In Spain it's timed to the bells of the Puerta del Sol on television; Mexico keeps the custom too.
- **example:** Este año sí logré comerme las doce uvas a tiempo.
  — *This year I actually managed to eat all twelve grapes in time.*

- **trap when producing Spanish:** An Italian who calls the night 'San Silvestre' will be understood but sounds foreign; the everyday words are 'Nochevieja' or, in Mexico, 'fin de año'.
